voice.text: All year we have explored Mowgli's jungle. [pause] But ecosystems can get hurt — by fire, by flood, and by people. [pause] Who can help an ecosystem stay healthy? Tap your guess.

Sometimes nature itself hurts an ecosystem. A fire burns the wood. A flood drowns the burrows. A disease spreads from animal to animal. [pause] But listen — not <emphasis>all</emphasis> fire is all bad. Some forests need a small fire now and then: it clears the old dry brush, and makes room for new green growth.

People can hurt ecosystems too — often without meaning to. [pause] Litter dumped in the stream hurts everyone downstream who drinks that water. Cutting every tree takes away homes and food. And wasting clean water leaves less for every living thing that needs it.

Remember your soil lesson? <emphasis>Erosion</emphasis> is the soil thief. [pause] When land is left bare — no grass, no roots — every hard rain steals some of the rich topsoil and washes it away. The hill loses its best layer, and the stream below turns muddy.

<emphasis>Conservation</emphasis> means protecting what the ecosystem needs — with counter-moves. [pause] Plant cover, so roots hold the soil. Use less water, so there is enough for all. Keep streams clean, so the water stays healthy. And where trees were cut — replant.

And here is the best part: every one of those counter-moves is one a kid can make. [pause] Turn off the tap. Pick up litter. Plant something green. [pause] The jungle we explored all year stays healthy when its caretakers — big and small — tend it. That includes you.
